teaching_point: Morbilliform (exanthematous) drug eruption — the commonest pattern; symmetrical truncal macules/papules 4–14 days after a new drug (aminopenicillins, sulfonamides, anticonvulsants, allopurinol). Check for SCAR red flags.

teaching_point: Close-up of confluent maculopapular drug exanthem — blanching, no mucosal involvement, no skin pain: usually stop drug, emollient + TCS, antihistamine.

teaching_point: Drug-induced urticaria — wheals within minutes–hours (penicillins, cephalosporins, NSAIDs, opioids, contrast). Ask about angioedema/anaphylaxis; document allergy precisely.

teaching_point: Toxic epidermal necrolysis — dusky, confluent, painful erythema that detaches; >30% BSA = TEN. Same-day emergency admission.

attribution: Image: DermNet — Toxic epidermal necrolysis (© DermNet) — https://dermnetnz.org/topics/stevens-johnson-syndrome-toxic-epidermal-necrolysis

teaching_point: Sheet-like epidermal detachment in TEN — Nikolsky-positive; count only detached/detachable skin for BSA/SCORTEN.
licence_note: DermNet image licence: https://dermnetnz.org/image-licence (watermarked low-res; personal/educational use with attribution)
attribution: Image: DermNet — Toxic epidermal necrolysis (© DermNet) — https://dermnetnz.org/topics/stevens-johnson-syndrome-toxic-epidermal-necrolysis

teaching_point: Haemorrhagic crusted lips in SJS/TEN.

teaching_point: Ocular involvement in SJS — ophthalmology review within 24 h of admission (BAD 2016); daily ocular care to prevent scarring.

teaching_point: Symblepharon — late ocular scarring after SJS/TEN; why early ophthalmology matters.

teaching_point: Nail shedding after TEN — long-term sequelae (nails, pigmentation, eyes, strictures) need follow-up.

teaching_point: Drug eruption on the legs (from DermNet's DRESS page) — DRESS presents as a morbilliform/infiltrated rash 2–8 weeks after the drug, with fever, facial oedema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, hepatitis (carbamazepine, allopurinol, lamotrigine).

attribution: Image: DermNet — Drug eruption (© DermNet) — https://dermnetnz.org/topics/drug-hypersensitivity-syndrome

teaching_point: AGEP — sheets of pinpoint non-follicular pustules on erythema within 1–2 days of a drug (often beta-lactams); fever, neutrophilia; resolves with superficial desquamation.

attribution: Image: DermNet — Acute generalised exanthematous pustulosis (© DermNet) — https://dermnetnz.org/topics/acute-generalised-exanthematous-pustulosis

teaching_point: AGEP on the trunk/flexures; DDx generalised pustular psoriasis.
licence_note: DermNet image licence: https://dermnetnz.org/image-licence (watermarked low-res; personal/educational use with attribution)
attribution: Image: DermNet — Acute generalised exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP) (© DermNet) — https://dermnetnz.org/topics/acute-generalised-exanthematous-pustulosis

teaching_point: ACE-inhibitor angioedema of the lip — bradykinin-mediated, no wheals/itch, poor response to antihistamine/steroid. Stop ACE-i permanently; airway first.

teaching_point: Erythema nodosum — tender, ill-defined red nodules on the shins (septal panniculitis). Oestrogen-containing COC is a recognised trigger.

teaching_point: Bilateral EN nodules evolving to bruise-like colour (erythema contusiformis); no ulceration, no scarring; 3–6 weeks. Unilateral EN (case) is atypical — exclude cellulitis/thrombophlebitis/DVT.

teaching_point: Blue-grey (slate) pigmentation of sun-exposed facial skin after long-term amiodarone. Fades over months–years after dose reduction/stop.
